about: The sheet for the Byrd Theatre cutaway: tools/cutaway/sheet.py. Callouts are anchored to drawn parts (history ids, in the isometric view and the flat section); each callout gives its badge's confidence. Callout text is working draft 3, written with Claude, for the artist to edit. The holly border and the red and green of the title and headings are sheet decoration, not part of the drawing.
title: The Byrd Theatre, Christmas Eve 1928
subtitle: Opening night, cut down the middle from the Cary Street doors to the screen, and across the stage
sectionCaption: The same cut, seen flat: Cary Street on the left, the stage on the right

callouts.title: The Cary Street front
callouts.text: Red brick and white terra cotta over granite and tan and black marble (nomination; RFP). The RFP lists five windows with striped canvas awnings (four drawn) and two flagpoles with ball finials.

callouts.title: The BYRD sign
callouts.text: Two storeys tall, designed by Fred Bishop, the architect and builder (RFP); lettered in the c. 1929 photograph, taken down in 1971 (foundation). Letter shapes approximate.

callouts.title: Marquee and box office
callouts.text: A pressed-copper marquee with lights in its ceiling (RFP), drawn blank: the nomination calls the original a plain bronze structure with no lettering. A black marble box office with two bronze speaker grilles; lobby-card cases at the corners (nomination; RFP).

callouts.title: Two sets of doors
callouts.text: Bronze doors with beveled glass (RFP), two sets of a dozen with the outer lobby between them (nomination).

callouts.title: Opening night
callouts.text: “A great civic event” (nomination). Evening seats 50 cents, matinees 25, children 10. The feature was a silent with sound added, the only picture left to book for the date, the general manager says (Style Weekly, 2014).

callouts.title: The lobby
callouts.text: A vaulted, gold-leafed ceiling 25 feet up, marble halfway up the walls, a mezzanine lounge on three sides (nomination), and crimson-and-gold Axminster carpet (foundation; RFP), drawn without its pattern.

callouts.title: Pool and fountain
callouts.text: Twenty feet by eight, with a fountain and fish (nomination; Rudisill 1986); a candy stand replaced it about 1940 (foundation). Place approximate.

callouts.title: Doors off the lobby
callouts.text: The manager’s office and restrooms off the lobby, more off the mezzanine (not drawn), and an office and vault at balcony level (RFP). Places approximate. The RFP’s candy closet is left out: candy came about 1940.

callouts.title: The seats
callouts.text: American Seating Company seats, 19 inches wide: cast-iron end standards with the aisle lights, rock-maple armrests, backs of gold and crimson mohair (foundation, Curator’s Corner, 2025). Rows approximate.

callouts.title: Balcony
callouts.text: 476 seats today. Emptied for new seats in 2025, it stood bare for the first time since 1928, the curator believes (Curator’s Corner). Depth and rake approximate.

callouts.title: Segregated
callouts.text: The Byrd is reported to have admitted no Black patrons until the 1960s (Wikipedia, citing a 2002 Richmond Times-Dispatch article not seen here). The Valentine records that Richmond's white-only theaters were desegregated in the 1960s. Nothing of this is drawn.

callouts.title: Dome, chandelier and colors
callouts.text: An oval dome (foundation) and the chandelier: four thousand crystals, three hundred bulbs, some two tons (nomination). The house lights ran in four colors: amber, white, red and blue (foundation), or red, blue, green and amber (press accounts).

callouts.title: Walls
callouts.text: Six murals by Arthur Brounet in niches and behind the boxes (nomination; foundation), not painted here, and silk damask panels (RFP) whose color is not recorded.

callouts.title: Projection booth
callouts.text: Two Simplex projectors, Vitaphone sound and the switchboard for every light (nomination; foundation); a rewind room and dimmer closet beside it (RFP). The manager calls it a small museum (Style Weekly, 2014).

callouts.title: Air tunnels and vents
callouts.text: Cooled air came through three concrete tunnels under the floor (foundation) and up through cast-iron “mushroom cap” vents under the seats (Curator’s Corner, 2025), from an air handler in the basement (RFP). Routes approximate.

callouts.title: The spring room
callouts.text: Past the boiler, a concrete opening overlooks a spring breached in the 1927 excavation and its pond, about 30 feet square (the general manager, Style Weekly, 2014; a 2019 account says 25). He says it never cooled the house and calls that the building’s favorite myth; Cinema Treasures and Wikipedia say it could or did. In Hurricane Isabel it rose to the boiler room door. His “backstage right” may mean either side: drawn house right.

callouts.title: Boiler and coal
callouts.text: Coal came from the alley through a coal door to the coal room and fed the boiler; its brick flue rises up the back wall (RFP). Places approximate.

callouts.title: The console’s lift
callouts.text: A screw lift in a shaft under the pit raises the console (RFP), the original Peter Clark lift (Rudisill 1986). The building shudders slightly as it starts, the house organist says (Richmond Family Magazine, 2015).

callouts.title: The console
callouts.text: Mahogany, four manuals, Wurlitzer Opus 1948, seventeen ranks (nomination; foundation). Carl Rhond played on opening night (Rudisill 1986). An eight-inch cable of thousands of wires runs to the organ’s rooms (RVA Mag, 2026).

callouts.title: Four rooms over the stage
callouts.text: Forty-odd steps up (Boomer, 2014): blower, Main, Solo and relay rooms, by the manager’s list (Style Weekly, 2014); some put the blower in the basement. Swell shutters open like blinds. The organist climbs up mid-show to free a stuck note (Boomer).

callouts.title: Proscenium and grille
callouts.text: A deep arch round the inner proscenium, covered in the 1950s (Rudisill 1986). A gold grille along it hides the organ’s openings (nomination).

callouts.title: Harp, piano and marimba
callouts.text: A piano in one box and a harp in the other, worked from the console (nomination). The harp, a Browne & Buckwell, does not play: a marimba below makes its sound (Richmond magazine, 2021). Which box held which is not known.

callouts.title: Drums over the screen
callouts.text: Drums, bells, a car horn, a bird whistle and tuned sleigh bells, played from the console (Richmond Family Magazine, 2015; Richmond magazine, 2021). Places approximate.

callouts.title: The sing-along
callouts.text: The house organist first heard it at twelve, in 1965, the bass rolling across the floor (Richmond Family Magazine, 2015). A patron born in 1939 remembers newsreels, cartoons and the sing-along (Yale Movie Memory Project, 2019).

callouts.title: A stage for pictures
callouts.text: Thirteen to fourteen feet deep, no dressing rooms, the alley about 15 feet behind the screen (Style Weekly, 2014; The Match, 2024); never a vaudeville house, the manager says. The curtain is drawn red, as in 1986.

callouts.title: The attic
callouts.text: An attic over the dome holds the theatre’s collection of 1928 plaster ornament (RFP).

sources: Sources: National Register nomination, Byrd Theatre (Virginia DHR 127-0287, 1977–79); Miles J. Rudisill Jr., Theatre Organ, Jan.–Feb. 1986, and its 1928 photographs; Byrd Theatre Foundation: About, Theatre History, The Mighty Wurlitzer Organ, Tours, Curator’s Corner (2025: seats, side sections, electrical), and its RFP for a general contractor (2026); Brent Baldwin, “Revising the Script”, Style Weekly, June 17, 2014 (the general manager’s walk-through); Richmond Family Magazine, June 29, 2015; Richmond magazine, April 18, 2021, and Dec. 1, 2006; Boomer, Dec. 5, 2014; RVA Mag, April 2, 2026; Mid-Atlantic Traveler, April 16, 2019; The Match, May 23, 2024; Yale Movie Memory Project, 2019; Cinema Treasures; Wikipedia, Byrd Theatre (it cites the Richmond Times-Dispatch, April 8, 2002, not seen); the Valentine, “Please Enjoy the Show” (Google Arts & Culture); the front c. 1929 (RVA Rephotography Project); OpenStreetMap contributors; USGS 3DEP lidar; City of Richmond, year of construction; National Weather Service; Museum District Association.
notes: No plan, section or seating chart was found, and the foundation’s 2024 Historic Structures Report was not seen: rooms are placed from written accounts and photographs inside the nomination’s 84 x 135 ft lot, which the OpenStreetMap outline matches within 0.2 m. Sources differ: 1,396 seats (the nomination, used here), 1,390 (1986) or 1,200 (the foundation today); 4,000 crystals and two tons, or 5,000 and two and a half; three organ chambers, two and a relay room, or four rooms; the four lamp colors; whether the spring ever served the air conditioning; whether the house was cooled in 1928 (the foundation says Carrier air from the start; a Cinema Treasures commenter remembers summer closures in the 1940s). The cut runs 5 ft east of the center line; the roof over the house and the ceiling beside the dome are lifted away. The pit is drawn narrow to leave room for the spring room beside it; the stage is drawn 14 ft deep. The street, the ground and the neighbors are today’s, a neighbor drawn only if the assessor dates it by 1928. No snow: none lay on the ground in Richmond on Christmas Day 1928 (Weather Service). No decorations are drawn in the building, since no account of any was found; the holly and the red and green of the title are the sheet’s own. Figures stand for no one in particular.
